place: support desk at one Fortune 500 software company, agents in several countries (study)
before: New agents took months to get good. The answers lived in the heads of a few veterans.
after: An assistant suggests replies drawn from the best agents' chats. The agent decides what to send. The least-skilled agents gained the most, about 36% more issues solved an hour.

before: Two radiologists read every mammogram, thousands a week.
after: Software sorts the scans and flags spots to look at. Radiologists make every call. In the 2025 analysis of about 106,000 women, they found 29% more cancers with 44% less reading.

before: Eight hours under bright lights watching brake rotors roll past, looking for hairline cracks. By the last hour of the shift, every rotor looks the same.
after: A camera flags anything that looks off. She pulls the flagged rotors and makes the call. When the tool starts rejecting good parts after a lighting change, she catches it.

place: trailer fabrication shop, Saint John, New Brunswick
before: Long runs of the same fillet weld on trailer frames, day after day, with the grinder and the fumes waiting at the end of each one.
after: A robot cell lays the repeat welds. He sets up each run and signs off on every frame. The hours it frees go to custom repair work and two apprentices, as the shop agrees in writing.

before: Feeding blanks into the same mill and checking every tenth part with calipers. One bad batch can mean a weekend of rework.
after: Sensors watch tool wear and stop the mill before parts drift. The machinist decides when to change tools, and when the system says a part is fine but the cut sounds wrong, she stops it anyway.

before: Fixing whatever breaks, usually at three in the morning, usually after it has already stopped the line.
after: Vibration sensors warn of a failing bearing days ahead. He decides which warnings are real and schedules the repair. His notes on each fix go into the system, and his contract pays him for them.

before: Rebuilding the weekly schedule by hand every time an order changes or a supplier runs late.
after: Software drafts the schedule in minutes. The planner walks the floor with the lead hands and fixes what it got wrong, like booking the finishing booth on the day it gets cleaned.

before: Measuring turbine blade profiles by hand and typing every reading into a spreadsheet. One inspection report takes most of a day.
after: A scanner measures each blade and writes the report. The technician signs it. When the scanner checks against an old revision of the drawing, he refuses to sign.

before: Grading every truckload by eye and hand at harvest, with farmers lined up down the road and the shift running past midnight.
after: An imaging grader gives a first read on each sample. The operator sets the final grade, and when a farmer disputes it, she walks him through the sample kernel by kernel.

before: Evenings at the kitchen table with yield maps and seed catalogues, working out what to plant where.
after: Software suggests a seeding plan field by field. He overrules it on the low quarter that floods every few springs, because he has watched it flood and the software hasn't.

before: Checking carcasses for contamination at a line speed that left no room to look twice.
after: Cameras flag the birds that need a second look. The inspector gives that second look and decides whether a lot gets held. Nobody on the line is ranked by what the cameras count.

before: Filling in catch logbooks by hand at the end of a fourteen-hour day on the water.
after: The electronic log fills itself from the GPS and the scale. The captain checks it before it goes in, and decides where to set traps from decades of knowing that bottom.

before: Long days drafting slides and analysis from scratch.
after: On work the tool was good at, consultants finished more, faster and better. On a task it was bad at, the ones who trusted it were 19 points less likely to be right.

before: Writing and reviewing code by hand on projects they knew inside out.
after: With AI tools they took 19% longer, while believing they were about 20% faster.

before: Up at four to watch each cow for signs of illness or heat, keeping track in a notebook that lives in the barn.
after: Collars track how each cow moves and eats and flag the ones that seem off. She decides who needs the vet. Her herd records stay hers, and the collar company has to ask before using them.

before: Walking the rows every morning checking leaves for pests, and adjusting heat and water from a clipboard.
after: Sensors run the climate and spot early pest damage. The grower decides when to spray and when to wait. When the system vents heat on a cold morning, he notices and has the setting fixed.

before: The first hour of every shift goes to charting and chasing medication records, before she says hello to a patient.
after: Notes draft themselves from her voice and the monitors. She reads and signs every one. That first hour goes to patients, like the man who is frightened about his surgery tomorrow.

place: long-term care home, North Bay, Ontario
before: Rushing between rooms with a paper list, then writing up the care log from memory at the end of the shift.
after: A tablet logs routine care as it happens. The minutes saved stay with residents, and the home writes that into its staffing plan instead of cutting a position.

before: Checking every prescription against interaction lists while the phone rings and the lineup grows.
after: Software flags interactions and drafts the counselling notes. The pharmacist decides what is real. When it clears two drugs as safe for a patient whose kidney results say otherwise, she catches it.

before: Hours a day re-checking image quality and sorting scans into the right queue for the radiologists.
after: The system sorts scans and suggests which look urgent. A radiologist still reads every image and signs every report. The tech has time to position patients properly and keep the nervous ones calm.

before: Patients wait weeks for a short visit, and half of that visit goes to typing.
after: A scribe tool drafts the visit notes while they talk. She checks and signs each one. The visit goes to the person in the chair, and her eyes stay off the screen.

before: Nineteen years of typing doctors' dictation, word for word. Speech software gets good enough that most of that typing is no longer needed.
after: She gets ninety days' notice in writing. Paid retraining, then first claim on the new role: checking machine-drafted notes for the mistakes only someone who has typed thousands of them would spot.

before: Hours on every new build cross-checking panel schedules against the drawings and marking up revisions by hand.
after: Software checks the drawings against the electrical code and flags conflicts. She decides which flags matter on site. When it reads a 15-amp circuit as 20, she spots it.

before: Writing quotes at the kitchen table after a full day of work, often for jobs he never gets.
after: An app drafts quotes from his photos and notes. He fixes the prices and the parts and gets his evenings back. The supplier behind the app pays him for the pricing data he agreed to share.

before: Daily reports and safety logs eat the mornings, so walking the site gets pushed to the afternoon.
after: Reports draft from photos and the crews' check-ins. He walks the site first thing. Every safety log still needs his signature, and he reads each one before he signs.

place: highway twinning project near Swift Current, Saskatchewan
before: Grading road bed by eye with a spotter, checking stakes, then regrading wherever the survey crew finds it off.
after: GPS guidance holds the grade. The operator still reads the ground. When the machine wants to cut through soft clay the model doesn't know about, he stops and calls the engineer.

place: heating and cooling company, St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador
before: Diagnosing heat pump faults by trial and error, sometimes three visits for one problem.
after: A diagnostic tool reads the unit and suggests a likely fault. The tech decides the fix, and keeps sharp by working the tricky ones by hand first, on paid training time the company sets aside.

before: Juggling forty trucks across the Prairies with a whiteboard and two phones, drivers calling in from the Trans-Canada.
after: Software builds routes and load plans. The dispatcher takes the calls that matter, like a driver saying he's too tired to push on. She backs him, and no driver is graded by the app.

before: Building next season's schedules in spreadsheets, trip by trip, over about six weeks.
after: Software drafts the schedule in a day. She spends the rest on what it misses, like the hospital shift change that packs the 7 bus at 6:45.

before: Ten hours a day walking the aisles with a scanner, pulling orders. Robots that bring the shelves to a station are coming, and most picking jobs with them.
after: He gets ninety days' notice in writing. The paid robotics course has twelve seats for forty pickers, and he doesn't get one. He leaves with severance above the legal minimum and looks for steady work.

before: Keying shipment details from paper invoices into customs forms, one truck at a time, while drivers wait at the line.
after: Software reads the invoices and fills the forms. The broker handles the shipments that don't fit. When it files tractor parts under the wrong tariff code, she catches it.

before: Planning where every container goes in the yard with a printout and a radio, then redoing it when a ship runs late.
after: Software plans the yard and the loading order. The planner overrules it when the weather turns or a crane crew is short, and every change shows up with her name on it.

before: Working out weight and balance by hand for every flight, with groceries and medicine competing for the same space.
after: Software does the weight and balance math. When there isn't room for everything, the agent decides what flies first. Medical supplies for a fly-in community go before anything that can wait a day.

place: regional grocery office, Dartmouth, Nova Scotia
before: Every Thursday, building orders from last year's sales reports and three binders of supplier specs.
after: A forecast drafts the order. The buyer knows the minor hockey tournament doubles chip sales in town that weekend, so she changes it, and her changes are visible to the stores.

before: Counting inventory and writing prep lists after close, when everyone just wants to go home.
after: Ordering and prep lists come out of the till system. The cook spends that hour teaching the new kid on the line, and the time saved goes to earlier finishes and a raise.

place: telecom call centre, Moncton, New Brunswick
before: Most calls are password resets and bill questions, handled from a script. A chatbot is set to take nearly all of them.
after: The team gets written notice, ninety days ahead. She retrains on paid time and moves to the escalations desk, where the angry and complicated calls go and someone has to listen.

before: Checking in a tour bus at once, typing passport details while the line backs up to the door.
after: Most guests check in on their phones. The clerk spends that time on the family whose flight landed at 2 a.m., and on the guest who needs a ground-floor room after knee surgery.

before: Writing up repair orders and phoning customers with quotes, back to back, while the bays wait.
after: A tool reads the technician's notes and drafts the quote. The advisor calls the customer herself and says which repairs can wait and which can't.

place: small accounting firm, Kelowna, British Columbia
before: Tax season means matching bank statements to receipts, line by line, well into the night.
after: Software matches the transactions and flags the odd ones. The accountant sits down with the client and asks the questions that matter, like whether that new truck is really a business expense.

before: Weeks before a hearing go to reading disclosure documents and tagging every page by hand.
after: A tool sorts and tags the documents. The paralegal checks its work. When it marks a key email as privileged and it isn't, she catches it. Every tag shows who made it, person or tool.

before: Cash and cheques at the wicket, eight hours a day. Most members have moved that banking to their phones.
after: Staff hear first, ninety days out. He applies for the new member advisor role and doesn't get it. He takes the severance and a paid retraining grant, and finishes a bookkeeping certificate while he looks for work.

place: claims office after a hailstorm, Calgary
before: Hundreds of claims after one storm, and weeks of driving house to house with a ladder and a clipboard.
after: Photos and drone images give a first estimate on simple claims. The adjuster goes in person on the hard ones, and no claim gets denied until a person has read the file.

before: Hundreds of applications for each opening, plus a constant back and forth of emails to book interviews.
after: Software sorts applications and books interviews, and it can't reject anyone. She reads every file it sets aside. That's how she finds it screening out welders for gaps in their work history.

before: Reading pay stubs and bank statements for every file and checking the math by hand.
after: The system reads the documents and checks the math. The underwriter makes the call on files that don't fit the usual box, like a fisher whose whole income lands between May and December.

before: Typing addresses and checking unit locations while trying to keep a panicking caller on the line.
after: The system finds the address and suggests the nearest unit. The dispatcher stays with the caller, talking a father through CPR until the paramedics are at the door.

before: Checking permit drawings against the building code page by page, with a three-month backlog.
after: Software screens drawings against the code first. The inspector makes every decision. When it passes a stair that is too steep, she catches it. With the backlog down, she spends more days on site.

place: child and family services, Thompson, Manitoba
before: More hours on case notes and forms than with the families on the caseload.
after: Notes draft from her recordings, with the family's consent. The tool can flag a concern but no score decides anything. She knows the family, and she makes the call with them.

before: Long hours at the desk cataloguing new books and processing holds and renewals.
after: Cataloguing and renewals mostly run themselves. The librarian runs a weekly drop-in for people who got a confusing letter from a government office and need help reading it.

place: provincial records office, Victoria, British Columbia
before: Twenty years of keying paper forms into the system and filing them. Most of those forms are moving online.
after: The office tells her a year ahead, well past the ninety days. She weighs retraining against severance, takes the severance and the training money, and enters a paid medical lab assistant program.

before: Checking eligibility rules across a stack of paperwork for each application, with phones ringing behind.
after: Software checks the paperwork and flags gaps. Only a person can deny an application. The worker spends more time on the hard cases, like a woman leaving a bad marriage with no paperwork at all.

before: Sunday nights marking spelling tests and math sheets, then planning the week from scratch.
after: Practice work marks itself. He reads every report card comment before it goes home and gets his Sundays back. Monday mornings go to the students who are falling behind.

before: Marking stacks of essays for grammar, with little time left to comment on the ideas.
after: A tool marks grammar and spelling. She writes comments on what each student is actually trying to say, and one essay a term is written by hand in class, so the skill stays.

before: Making an adapted version of every worksheet by hand for students with different needs.
after: A tool drafts adapted worksheets, including versions in Inuktitut. The assistant and an Elder check every one before it reaches a student, and the Elder is paid for that review.

before: Grading theory quizzes and writing new tests every term for each section.
after: Quizzes mark themselves. The instructor spends those hours in the shop, watching students weld and correcting their angle before a bad habit sets in.

place: community learning centre, Corner Brook, Newfoundland and Labrador
before: Hours each week hunting for reading material adults would actually want to read, at the right level.
after: A tool pulls articles about hunting season and hockey and rewrites them at the right level. The tutor checks each one, then sits beside the learner while he reads it aloud.

before: After an ice storm, driving back roads looking for downed lines one concession at a time.
after: Smart meters and drones show where the outages are. The crew lead decides the order of repairs, and she puts a dairy farm with a failing generator ahead of what the software ranks first.

before: Checking gas readings and ground conditions by hand, shift after shift, a kilometre down.
after: Sensors read the gas and the ground all shift. The shift boss decides whether a drift is safe to enter, and pulls crews out when the readings look fine and the rock doesn't sound right.

before: Weeks cruising timber on foot, measuring trees plot by plot for the harvest plan.
after: Lidar maps the stand from the air. The forester walks the plots that matter. When the plan marks caribou calving ground for cutting, she finds it and the cut is moved.

place: oil sands upgrader, Fort McMurray, Alberta
before: Watching dozens of screens through a twelve-hour night shift, waiting for the one alarm that mattered.
after: Software filters nuisance alarms and suggests responses. The operator makes every call on the plant. His crew's know-how goes into the alarm rules, with their names on them and a bonus attached.

before: Logging water levels and turbine readings on paper every hour through the night.
after: Readings log on their own. The operator spends the shift walking the station and teaching new hires what a bearing sounds like before it fails.

before: Hours transcribing interviews and council meeting recordings before writing a word.
after: Transcripts come back in minutes. The reporter checks every quote against the tape before it runs. When the software puts a councillor's words in the mayor's mouth, she catches it.

before: Resizing the same ad into forty formats for every campaign, pixel by pixel.
after: Software handles the resizes. The designer spends the time on the idea and still checks every version, because the tool sometimes crops the product out of the small ones.

before: Translating government reports from English to French, page by page. Machine translation starts producing first drafts of most of them.
after: The firm gives staff ninety days' notice. She retrains on paid time as a reviser and signs off before anything is published. The work left is where one wrong word changes what a law means.

before: Days of logging footage, marking every shot by hand before the real edit could start.
after: Software logs the footage. The editor shapes the story. When the tool tags part of an Elder's interview as silence, she knows that pause is the best moment in the film.

before: Running the same regression tests by hand before every release, clicking through the same screens.
after: Automated tests run overnight. The tester spends the day trying to break the app the way real people do: one bar of signal, a cracked screen, a Friday rush.

place: regional health authority, Prince George, British Columbia
before: Hundreds of tickets a week, most of them locked accounts and printer jams.
after: A chatbot clears the routine tickets. The tech spends her days at the nursing stations, sorting out the problems that slow down care.

before: Sifting through thousands of security alerts a day, almost all of them false alarms.
after: Software sorts the alerts and drafts incident reports. The analyst decides what's a real attack. When the system files one as routine because it looks like a normal login, he spots it.

before: Writing the same boilerplate code for every new feature, then hunting down typos in it.
after: A coding assistant writes the routine code. The developer reviews every line before it ships, and keeps one day a sprint for writing code by hand, so she can still tell when the assistant is wrong.
